rationale:
The example `requirements.sdk.graph.hierarchical-paths` describes a concrete case with a stated expected result. The requirement `a.b.c` is represented as `ReviewNodeId::Requirement(vec!["a","b","c"])`. Its `node_path` is `["requirement","a","b","c"]`.

The supplied test is `crates/trust-but-verify/src/graph/validation_tests.rs#fn[enum_node_ids_distinguish_requirements_and_source_items_in_one_domain]`. It carries a `{test}` reference to the example. It defines the `ReviewNodeId` enum with `Requirement(Vec<String>)` and `Source{file,selector}` variants, and a `Domain` implementation whose `node_path` prepends "requirement" to the parts.

The test builds `ReviewNodeId::Requirement(vec!["a","b","c"])`. It asserts `Domain::node_path(&domain,&hierarchical).segments()` equals `["requirement","a","b","c"]`. That is the example's exact input and expected output.

The test also checks the cited `requirements.sdk.graph.node_path_method` obligations that apply to this case:
- Converting the same id twice gives equal paths.
- A fresh `ReviewDomain::default()` gives the same path, which covers stability across runs.
- The requirement and source ids get different paths: `["requirement","sdk","errors"]` against `["source","src/lib.rs","fn[validate]"]`.

I found no outcome in the example that the test leaves unasserted. The example is illustrative of a user-defined domain, so a test-local domain implementation is an appropriate way to check it.
